place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 告示栏
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the notice board

setup.zh: 开山门那一夜：女弟子的大通铺上，一个红鼻头的姑娘在小本子上记账；男弟子的大通铺上，马小宝跟两个老弟子嘀咕到半夜。告示栏上，墨迹未干。
setup.en: The night the gate opened: on the girls' long bunk, a red-nosed girl keeps accounts in her little notebook; on the boys', Ma Xiaobao whispers with two old disciples past midnight. On the notice board, the ink is not yet dry.

recap.zh: 外门第一夜：马小宝成了「马师兄」，告示栏上贴出公中告示——每人先交一块。
recap.en: The first night in the outer court: Ma Xiaobao became "Senior Brother Ma", and the common-fund notice went up — one stone each, paid first.

zh: 外门的告示栏，墨迹未干。
en: The outer court's notice board, ink still wet.

story.zh:
话分两头。外门女弟子的大通铺，在另一个院子里。那一夜熄灯以前，阿禾坐在铺上，把袄子的衬里拆开一道缝，一粒一粒地数里头的谷子。数到末了，二十九。她又数了一遍，还是二十九。

她没吭声，把袄子穿上，出了院子。夜里的山门静得很，石阶上一个人也没有，只有第三百级上，还有一下一下的沙沙声——那扫地的老头还在扫。阿禾走过去，蹲下来，就着月光，一级一级往下找。往下找了三级，那老头的扫帚停在她面前，扫帚底下，压着一粒谷子。

老头弯腰把那粒谷子捡起来，搁在她手心里，道：「种的？」阿禾道：「种的。」老头道：「山上的地，薄。」阿禾道：「家里的地，也薄。」老头看了她一会儿，没再说话，又扫地了。阿禾把那粒谷子缝回衬里，缝了三针，打了个死结。

回到铺上，她那一张最靠墙。她点起一盏豆大的油灯，趴在灯底下，拿一截新削的炭条，在那个蓝布面的小本子上，一笔一画地写：

九月初九。重阳。

九个数。没人教我口诀。一到九，在本子上加一遍，四十五。分三份，十五。先算总数，再摆。

林子。我闭着眼睛进去的。看了要记，记了要怕。不看。

他往右滚那一下，像是有人跟他说了什么。记：问。不问。先记着。

马家的人往林子里扔了一颗石子。我看见了。扫地的老头也看见了。记。

他喊了我三回。我没应。考试的时候，不认人。

爹在山门外头站了一天，一口没吃。记：爹，别替我还账。

五两。弟弟。

禾种三十粒，缝在袄里。

记：沈小满，欠我鸡蛋三个半。

男弟子的大通铺上，鼾声一片。小满睡在最靠门的那张铺上，门缝里的风一夜往里灌。靠窗最好的那张铺，是马小宝的。他的家丁不许在山上过夜，傍晚便下山去了，可天黑以后，另有两个上一届的老弟子，嘴里带着酒气，蹲在他铺边上压着嗓子说话。小满只听清了几句：「……新来的一百多个，一人一块……」「……头一个月，三成归你……」「……那个杂灵根——」马小宝的声音：「他那块，我亲自收。」

小满旁边那张铺上，孙二狗也没睡，翻过身来，小声道：「明天那一块，你交不交？」小满道：「你呢？」孙二狗想了一想：「我交最小的那一块。」说完，翻回去，一会儿就打起了呼噜。

小满把胸口的木牌掏出来，握在手心里。这一整天，它只烫了一回，就两个字，「左边」。今天是重阳，他娘在家里大约也插了茱萸，插完了数一数，少一个人。他对着木牌，小声说道：「现在打不过。他有荐书，有人，有他家的钱。我什么都没有。」停了一停，又道：「可是——账，我都记着呢。」

握在手心里的木牌，轻轻地，暖了一下。

窗外，外门的告示栏上，贴着一张新的告示，墨迹还没干：

**外门公中：新入门弟子，领了灵石，每人先交一块。明日一早，饭堂门口。**

落款三个字：马师兄。写这三个字的人，进山门还不到半天。
story.en:
Meanwhile, elsewhere. The girls' long bunk of the outer court was in another courtyard. That night, before the lamps went out, Ahe sat on her bunk, unpicked a seam in the lining of her jacket, and counted the grains inside one by one. At the end: twenty-nine. She counted again: still twenty-nine.

She said nothing, put her jacket on, and went out of the courtyard. The gate was very quiet at night, no one on the stair, only on the three hundredth step a steady *shh, shh* — the old sweeper was still sweeping. Ahe went over, squatted, and in the moonlight searched down step by step. Three steps down, the old man's broom stopped in front of her, and under the broom lay one grain.

The old man bent, picked up the grain, and put it in her palm. "For sowing?" Ahe said, "For sowing." The old man said, "The land up here is thin." Ahe said, "The land at home's thin too." The old man looked at her a while, said no more, and swept again. Ahe sewed the grain back into the lining — three stitches and a knot that wouldn't come undone.

Back at the bunk — hers was nearest the wall — she lit a lamp the size of a bean, lay under it with a freshly sharpened stick of charcoal, and wrote stroke by stroke in the blue-cloth notebook:

The ninth of the ninth. Double Ninth.

Nine numbers. Nobody taught me a rhyme. One to nine, added once in the book: forty-five. Split three ways: fifteen. Reckon the total first, then set the stones.

The forest. I went in with my eyes shut. Look, and you remember; remember, and you're afraid. So don't look.

That roll of his to the right — like someone told him something. Noted: ask. Don't ask. Note it for now.

Someone of the Mas threw a pebble into the forest. I saw. The old sweeper saw too. Noted.

He called me three times. I didn't answer. During the trials I don't know anybody.

Dad stood outside the gate all day and didn't eat a bite. Noted: Dad, don't pay my debts for me.

Five taels. Little brother.

Thirty grains of seed rice, sewn into my jacket.

Noted: Shen Xiaoman owes me three and a half eggs.

On the boys' long bunk, snoring everywhere. Xiaoman slept in the bed nearest the door, the draught through the crack blowing in all night. The best bed, by the window, was Ma Xiaobao's. His servants weren't allowed to stay the night on the mountain and had gone down at dusk; but after dark two old disciples from the last intake, breath smelling of wine, squatted by his bed talking low. Xiaoman caught only a few words: "…the hundred-odd new ones, one each…" "…first month, thirty in the hundred is yours…" "…that mixed root —" Ma Xiaobao's voice: "His, I'll collect myself."

On the bed beside Xiaoman, Sun Ergou wasn't asleep either; he turned over and whispered: "That one stone tomorrow — will you pay?" Xiaoman said, "Will you?" Sun Ergou thought a moment. "I'll pay the smallest one." And he turned back, and in a moment was snoring.

Xiaoman took the token from his chest and held it in his palm. All day it had burned once, two words: "Left." Today was Double Ninth; at home his mother would have put up dogwood, and counted when she'd done, and been one short. He said softly to the token: "Can't beat them now. He's got a letter, got people, got his family's money. I've got nothing." He stopped a moment, and said again: "But — I'm keeping the books on all of it."

The token in his palm, gently, warmed once.

Outside the window, on the outer court's notice board, a new notice had been posted, the ink not yet dry:

**Outer court common fund: new disciples, once you draw your spirit stones, pay one each first. Tomorrow morning, at the refectory door.**

Signed with three characters: Senior Brother Ma. The one who wrote them had been inside the gate less than half a day.

exits.means: rests, ends the day, or asks what comes next
